items.topic: VRE/MDRO — Contact Precautions (gown and gloves) in acute care
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: A hospitalized client is colonized with vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE). Which infection-control action is most appropriate in acute care?

options.text: Place the client on Contact Precautions and wear a gown and gloves for care involving contact with the client or environment
Use Airborne Precautions with a negative-pressure room and N95 for all VRE colonization
No PPE is needed because colonization never transmits in hospitals
Use Droplet Precautions with a surgical mask only and leave the door open to the hallway

rationales.A: Correct. CDC Appendix A lists MDROs including VRE for Contact + Standard Precautions when judged clinically/epidemiologically significant; OpenStax lists VRE among MDROs and Contact Precautions require gown and gloves.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Airborne/AIIR is not the routine category for VRE colonization.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Contact transmission of MDROs is a recognized healthcare risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Droplet-only PPE does not address contact/environmental transmission of VRE.

sources.title: Appendix A: Type and Duration of Precautions
sources.publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sources.evidence: MDROs including VRE: Contact + Standard Precautions when judged of clinical/epidemiologic significance; Contact recommended in acute care settings with increased transmission risk.

sources.section: Contact Precautions; Dealing with Multidrug-Resistant Organisms
sources.evidence: Examples of MDROs include VRE; Contact Precautions PPE includes gloves and isolation gown whenever touching the patient; discard before exiting.

items.topic: NGN matrix — VRE Contact Precautions actions indicated vs not
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: For a client on Contact Precautions for VRE colonization in acute care, indicate whether each action is Indicated or Not indicated.

Prefer a single-patient room when available
Remove PPE before exiting the room and perform hand hygiene
Place the client in a negative-pressure AIIR solely because of VRE colonization

rationales.R5: Not indicated. Asymptomatic colonization still warrants Contact PPE in acute care when indicated.

items.topic: Latex allergy — provide latex-free / alternative gloves for allergic staff or clients
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: A nurse reports a latex allergy. Which workplace action best protects the nurse while maintaining infection-control barriers?

options.text: Provide readily accessible suitable non-latex (or otherwise appropriate alternative) gloves so barrier protection continues without latex exposure
Require continued powdered latex gloves because ‘hypoallergenic’ always means latex-free
Stop all glove use for blood exposure tasks so the allergy resolves
Only wear latex gloves inside-out to neutralize proteins

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: use latex-free alternatives such as neoprene or vinyl for latex sensitivity. OSHA BBP: hypoallergenic gloves, liners, powderless gloves, or similar alternatives shall be readily accessible to employees allergic to the gloves normally provided.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Hypoallergenic labeling must not be assumed to mean latex-free.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Barrier protection is still required for blood/OPIM exposure.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Inside-out latex still exposes the wearer to latex proteins.

sources.title: 10.4 Infection Control and Patient Safety
sources.evidence: If latex sensitivity is indicated, use alternative products such as latex-free gloves made of neoprene or vinyl.

items.topic: Pharyngeal diphtheria — Droplet Precautions until cultures negative after therapy
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: A client is admitted with suspected pharyngeal diphtheria. Which isolation plan is correct?

options.text: Use Droplet Precautions (with Contact as indicated) and continue until the client is off effective antimicrobial therapy and follow-up cultures are negative per guidance
No isolation is needed because diphtheria is only foodborne
Use Airborne Precautions in an AIIR for the entire hospital stay regardless of cultures
Use Contact Precautions only for 2 hours after the first antibiotic dose, then discontinue all precautions

rationales.A: Correct. CDC Appendix A: pharyngeal diphtheria — Droplet + Standard until off antimicrobial treatment and culture-negative (2 cultures 24 h apart). Merck: isolation with respiratory-droplet (and contact) precautions until sequential cultures after antibiotics are negative.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Respiratory diphtheria spreads by droplets/secretions.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Routine category is Droplet (+ Contact as indicated), not indefinite Airborne/AIIR solely for diphtheria.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Precautions continue until treatment completion and culture clearance criteria are met.

sources.title: Appendix A: Type and Duration of Precautions
sources.publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sources.evidence: Diphtheria Pharyngeal: Droplet + Standard until off antimicrobial treatment and culture-negative; until 2 cultures taken 24 hours apart negative.

sources.title: Diphtheria
sources.evidence: Isolation with respiratory-droplet and contact precautions required until 2 sequential cultures after antibiotics are stopped are negative.

items.topic: Dumping syndrome — smaller, more frequent meals and decreased carbohydrate intake
items.stem: After gastric resection, a client develops postprandial weakness, sweating, dizziness, and palpitations suggestive of dumping syndrome. Which dietary teaching is most appropriate?

options.text: Eat smaller, more frequent meals and decrease carbohydrate (especially hyperosmolar/high-sugar) intake
Drink large volumes of sugary soda with every large meal to ‘dilute’ the stomach contents
Eat only two very large high-carbohydrate meals daily
Replace all meals with undiluted fruit juice boluses for rapid emptying

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: dumping after gastric surgery — dietary modifications with smaller, more frequent meals and decreased carbohydrate intake usually help. MedlinePlus post–gastric bypass: eat 6 small meals; avoid foods/drinks high in sugar/carbohydrates; do not drink while eating.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Sugary liquids with large meals worsen dumping/hyperosmolar symptoms.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Large high-carbohydrate meals provoke dumping.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Rapid carbohydrate boluses worsen symptoms.

items.topic: Parkinson disease — promote safety and reduce fall risk (balance/home adaptations)
items.stem: A client with Parkinson disease has impaired balance and a shuffling gait. Which nursing action best reduces fall risk?

options.text: Teach fall-prevention strategies and support home safety adaptations (for example grab bars) while maximizing safe activity
Encourage running on wet floors without assistive devices to ‘challenge balance’
Remove all lighting so the client learns to walk in the dark
Keep pathways cluttered with cords to build agility

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: therapists may teach adaptive strategies and home adaptations (e.g., grab bars) to reduce fall risk while maximizing activity. OpenStax: environments should promote safety and help clients avoid falls and other hazards.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Unsafe challenge increases fall/injury risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Poor lighting increases fall risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Clutter and cords are fall hazards.

items.topic: Suspected ACS/MI — chewed non–enteric-coated aspirin 160–325 mg unless contraindicated
items.stem: A client arrives with suspected acute coronary syndrome. Unless contraindicated, which antiplatelet action is appropriate on arrival?

options.text: Give non–enteric-coated aspirin 160–325 mg for the client to chew (then swallow) to speed absorption
Give only enteric-coated aspirin 81 mg to swallow whole without chewing, and delay any antiplatelet therapy for 24 hours
Never give aspirin in ACS because it always worsens thrombosis
Administer aspirin as an intramuscular injection into the deltoid for fastest effect

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: all patients given aspirin 160–325 mg (not enteric-coated) if not contraindicated; chewing the first dose quickens absorption. OpenStax: administer 325 mg aspirin for platelet aggregation in MI care.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Initial ACS dosing is chewed non–enteric-coated 160–325 mg, not delayed enteric 81 mg only.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Early aspirin reduces mortality risk in ACS/MI.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Oral chewed aspirin is the standard initial route described here, not IM.

sources.title: Medications for Acute Coronary Syndromes
sources.evidence: Aspirin 160–325 mg (not enteric-coated) if not contraindicated; chewing the first dose before swallowing quickens absorption; reduces short- and long-term mortality risk.

sources.title: 12.5 Myocardial Infarction
sources.evidence: Administer 325 mg aspirin for platelet aggregation; common acute antiplatelet therapy is aspirin 325 mg.

items.topic: NGN bowtie — suspected ACS: chewed aspirin; monitor perfusion/bleeding cues
items.stem: A client with crushing chest pain and suspected ACS is being treated on arrival. Complete the bowtie: the priority condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Suspected acute coronary syndrome needing urgent antiplatelet therapy
Uncomplicated seasonal allergic rhinitis without chest pain
Resolved ankle sprain awaiting discharge teaching only
Dietary preference for caffeine without cardiac symptoms

actions.text: Give non–enteric-coated aspirin 160–325 mg for the client to chew unless contraindicated
Initiate continuous cardiac monitoring and support oxygenation/perfusion per protocol
Delay all evaluation for 48 hours to see if pain resolves spontaneously
Tell the client to run a marathon immediately to ‘open the arteries’
Give only intramuscular aspirin into the buttocks as first-line therapy

parameters.text: Chest pain, ECG changes, and hemodynamic/perfusion status
Bleeding cues (e.g., bruising, GI bleeding signs) while on antiplatelet therapy

rationales.K1: Correct. Crushing chest pain with suspected ACS is the priority condition.
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Ankle sprain is unrelated to ACS care.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Dietary caffeine alone is not the priority.
rationales.A1: Correct. Chewed non–enteric-coated aspirin 160–325 mg unless contraindicated (Merck/OpenStax).
rationales.A2: Correct. OpenStax: telemetry/hemodynamic monitoring and oxygenation/perfusion support are key acute MI nursing actions.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Initial therapy described is oral chewed aspirin, not IM.
rationales.P1: Correct. Monitor ischemic and perfusion status.
rationales.P2: Correct. OpenStax notes monitoring for bleeding/bruising on antiplatelet therapy.

sources.title: Medications for Acute Coronary Syndromes
sources.evidence: Aspirin 160–325 mg chewed (not enteric-coated) unless contraindicated.

sources.title: 12.5 Myocardial Infarction
sources.evidence: Aspirin 325 mg; maintain oxygenation/perfusion monitoring; monitor for bleeding/bruising on antiplatelet therapy.

items.topic: Five Rights of Delegation — right task, circumstance, person, communication, supervision
items.stem: Which statement best reflects the Five Rights of Nursing Delegation?

options.text: Delegation decisions should address the right task, right circumstance, right person, right communication/directions, and right supervision/evaluation
Once a task is delegated, the RN has no accountability for patient outcomes
Any unstable critical-care task may be freely delegated without assessing competence
The Five Rights replace the need for facility policies and nurse practice act compliance

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax and NCSBN/ANA National Guidelines list the Five Rights: right task, circumstance, person, communication/directions, and supervision/evaluation.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The RN retains accountability for appropriate delegation and outcomes.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Right circumstance requires stable/appropriate conditions; competence must be verified.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Delegation still must comply with law, standards, and employer policy.

items.topic: NGN cloze — Five Rights of Delegation components
items.stem: Complete the teaching about safe nursing delegation using the Five Rights.

ngn.template: Before delegating, the RN confirms the {B1}, ensures the {B2}, verifies the {B3} is competent, provides clear {B4}, and plans {B5}.

B2.text: right circumstance (patient sufficiently stable for the delegation)

B4.text: silence with no opportunity for questions
vague instructions only after the shift ends

B5.text: right supervision and evaluation of outcomes
abandonment of the unit with no follow-up
ignoring abnormal findings reported by the delegatee

rationales.B1a: Correct. Right task is within job description/policies (OpenStax/NCSBN).
rationales.B2a: Correct. Right circumstance requires appropriate patient condition/stability.
rationales.B3a: Correct. Right person with verified competence.
rationales.B4a: Correct. Clear directions/communication with opportunity for questions.
rationales.B4b: Incorrect. Communication must be clear and two-way.
rationales.B4c: Incorrect. Timing/clarity must support safe performance.
rationales.B5a: Correct. Right supervision and evaluation of outcomes.
rationales.B5c: Incorrect. RN must respond to concerning findings.

items.jurisdiction_note: O. Reg. 799/93 s.1 item 15 + CNO Documentation
items.topic: Ontario — signing/issuing a false or misleading professional document is misconduct
items.stem: An Ontario nurse is asked to sign a letter that intentionally misstates a client’s clinical status. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Signing or issuing, in a professional capacity, a document the nurse knows or ought to know contains a false or misleading statement is professional misconduct
False statements are acceptable if the employer requests them for convenience
Only physicians can commit documentation-related professional misconduct in Ontario
Nurses may knowingly issue misleading documents if no one is expected to read them

rationales.A: Correct. O. Reg. 799/93 lists signing/issuing a known false or misleading professional document as misconduct. CNO Documentation likewise prohibits falsifying records and signing/issuing documents with false or misleading statements.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Employer convenience does not authorize false professional documents.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Nursing Act regulation applies to nurses.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Knowingly issuing false/misleading documents is misconduct regardless of expected readership.

sources.title: O. Reg. 799/93 Professional Misconduct
sources.evidence: Signing or issuing, in the member’s professional capacity, a document that the member knows or ought to know contains a false or misleading statement is professional misconduct.

sources.title: Documentation
sources.section: Documentation requirements — falsify / false or misleading statement
sources.evidence: Nurses do not falsify a record relating to their practice, including signing or issuing a document that they know or ought to know includes a false or misleading statement.
